chunks: He narrated from Ibn Ribat, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about two men, for each of whom there is food with the other's companion, and one does not know how much he has on the other, nor does the other know how much he has on the first. He said: 'Each of them says to his companion: 'For you is what is with you, and for me is what is with me,' and they both agreed to that.' He said: 'There is no harm if they agree to that and their souls are pleased with it.'

key_terms.صَاحِبِهِ: Companion/Partner (referring to the other party in the transaction)
key_terms.طَابَتْ بِهِ أَنْفُسُهُمَا: Their souls were pleased with it (indicating contentment and lack of regret)
key_terms.طَعَامٌ: Food (used here as a general term for goods/commodities in trade)
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm (a legal term indicating permissibility)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on exchanging goods when both parties are unsure of the exact quantity held by the other?
ai.summary: In the context of *al-Shirka* (partnership) and *al-Mudaraba* (profit-sharing) in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, this narration establishes the validity of *Sulh* (amicable settlement) to resolve uncertainty (*Gharar*) through mutual consent. The Imam’s ruling emphasizes that if both parties are satisfied (*tabitat bihi anfusuhuma*) with the exchange of what is currently in their possession, the transaction is legally sound, reflecting the Shia principle that consent can mitigate minor uncertainties in commercial dealings.
